line: d4 Nf6 Bf4 c5 e3 d5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Qa5+
teaches: A system opening's strength is its routine — the same setup in the same order every game. The early queen check is the interruption: it arrives before the routine finishes, and every answer costs something the system wanted to keep. Against a setup player, the question beats the scheme.
explains: The queen checks from a5 at the king still on e1, and the routine stops: blocking commits a piece to a square it did not want, and the alternatives disturb the setup's order. The system player is out of their script on move six.

line: d4 Nf6 Bf4 c5 e3 d5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 Qa5+ Nc3 Bg4
teaches: In these solid setups one knight glues the position together — it holds the centre pawn and covers the squares the setup depends on. The pin against the queen freezes that knight, and greed can wait: developing every piece against a tangled position wins more than any pawn on offer.
explains: The bishop on g4 attacks the knight on f3 and pins it against the queen. The knight holds the centre together, and while it is stuck the development race is running in only one direction — the pawn-grabs on offer are worth less than the next developing move.
